OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $G$ be a graph given by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where any two distinct points are at least distance $1$ apart, and we draw an edge between two points if they are distance $1$ apart.
Let $g(n)$ be maximal such that any such graph always has an independent set on at least $g(n)$ vertices. Estimate $g(n)$, or perhaps $\lim \frac{g(n)}{n}$.
#1066: [Er87b,p.171]
graph theory | 
planar graphs
Such graphs are always planar. Erdős initially thought that $g(n)=n/3$, but Chung and Graham, and independently Pach, gave a construction that shows $g(n)\leq \frac{6}{19}n$. Pach and Toth [PaTo96] improved this to $g(n)\leq \frac{5}{16}n$.
Pollack [Po85] noted that the Four colour theorem implies $g(n)\geq n/4$, since the graph is planar. Pollack reports that Pach observed that this in for unit distance graphs the four colour theorem can be proved by a simple induction. 
This lower bound has been improved to $\frac{9}{35}n$ by Csizmadia [Cs98] and then $\frac{8}{31}n$ by Swanepoel [Sw02]. The current record bounds are therefore\[\frac{8}{31}n \approx 0.258n \leq g(n) \leq 0.3125n=\frac{5}{16}n.\]Pollack [Po85] also reports a letter from Erdős which poses the more general problem of, given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with minimum distance $1$, let $g_d(n)$ be maximal such that there always exist at least $g_d(n)$ many points which have minimum distance $>1$. Is it true that $g_d(n) \gg n/d$ in general? The upper bound $g_d(n) \ll n/d$ is trivial, considering widely spaced unit simplices.
See [1070] for the general estimate of independence number of unit distance graphs.

 Also the improved 6/23 bound has been written up as an unconditional proof. It is a modest improvement over the previous $\frac{7}{27}n$ bound, and the new note supersedes the earlier proof.
This improvement was completely autonomously done with GPT-5.6 Sol Pro, nudging it to improve past the $\frac{7}{27}n$ bound, with manual and agentic work to improve the exposition of the resulting note. To be honest, the improved bounds and methods are of little mathematical insight in terms of proof route, but rather a collection of curiosities that nonetheless require thorough review over many apparently "trivial" statements.
Much of the progress is essentially doing the dirty work more thoroughly than the previous improvement, with more local analysis pushed further. The important change here is the use of equality in the expansion estimates to force additional lattice vertices. In any case, the newly set bound is in my eyes non-trivial, and a genuine improvement. The Csizmadia machinery keeps delivering still.
As a (personal) conjecture, I currently expect that $\lim \frac{g(n)}{n}$ also will resolve to $\frac{5}{16}$. Proving this might provide some insight or estimates about specific colourings of such graphs in and of itself. Or, conversely, this might just require proving such colourings to be possible or impossible, thereby proving the necessary lower bound of this problem.
In any case, I would be suprised if the current methodology can improve the lower bound far enough to settle the eventual limit.

 I am wondering what a meaningful contribution to this problem is, or for that matter what solving this problem beyond currently improving bounds. I believe it is possible to inch this lower bound further, but I am wondering in what capacity this would contribute. Specifically, I believe a lower bound of 7/27 can be pushed with most of the same machinery as Swanepoel with tedious work for a reduction to m=7.
However, I would like some input by those more familiar with the subject. What constitutes a meaningful contribution here? 
I am still currently working on formalizing the current best bounds, and only then working on stricter bounds since I find the current arguments via induction precarious and difficult. I have added all GPT-5.5 pro conversations related to solving this problem, which mostly tend to agree that the current arguments hold, up to the imported machinery of Swanepoel's methodology. I have tried my best to make sure that the current mathematics holds up to that standard!
I won't be able to 100% guarrantee full correctness for this attempt because it's genuinely hard for me to work through, but this is also not the final attempt yet. I am currently working up a formalization of the original bounds of the Pach and Toth paper and the Swanepoel paper, which has turned out to be quite the challenge (200k lines of Lean right now...). After I can even certify Swanepoels inputs and the full cited lemmas and theorems, I am quite confident my current write up suffices.
I believe I have a genuine result worth sharing. Don't waste too much time working through this proof please, this is at best a good reference note I know has issues.
Thanks for reading my update :D

For those interested in full workflow details, this one was a bit special!
For this problem, my current workflow includes a cross-auditing of having a half-hallucinating GPT-5.5 Pro with iterative audits against it to try to validate that no smallest counterexample to this new lower bound can exist. Current versions of GPT 5.5 Pro either woefully refuse to do any work on this problem, or manage to hallucinate their way into careless theorems and lemmas. Only way I managed so far was explicitly forbidding it from making any attempt at saying it cannot solve the problem and go from there. Quite an interesting workflow if I'm honest, I see this improving in a few months.
Essentially, since current models (aka GPT-5.5 pro) refuse to work without explicit targets or bounds, I ran a mostly empirical method of new upper and lower bound selections, first trying for a bound of 2/7 which required proving a four-coloring configuration I couldn't work my way through. Eventually, one of the many GPT-5.5 pro hallucinations turned to 7/27 via badly constructed machinery which I identified as a plausible route, which over the course of 4 days has turned into this attempt.
